fields.hint: The pool serves fs, zlib, dns.lookup and some crypto calls. A file wait and a pbkdf2 burst load it in very different ways.
fields.explanation: More threads help only if the pool is the real bottleneck and the machine has spare cores. On a 4-CPU box, eight concurrent pbkdf2 calls took about 750 ms with UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=1 and about 210 ms at the default 4, while raising it to 8 or 32 changed nothing, because the cores were already busy. So identify the queued operations (fs, zlib, dns.lookup, pbkdf2/scrypt) and test a bounded change against your own load and hardware. A fixed value set everywhere cannot match every machine, CPU count is not the rule for I/O-bound file work, and the synchronous variants skip the pool only by blocking the event loop instead.

hint restates the first half of the key ('find which of yours queues' vs key 'Find which calls are queueing')
evidence: node: RSS after 8 pbkdf2 - UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE=4: 45MB, =128: 46MB, =1024: 53MB, so the memory-waste line was also unsupported

https://nodejs.org/en/learn/asynchronous-work/dont-block-the-event-loop: Worker Pool serves dns.lookup/lookupService, all fs APIs except FSWatcher and the synchronous ones, crypto.pbkdf2/scrypt/randomBytes/randomFill/generateKeyPair and non-synchronous zlib; more Workers than logical cores 'provides no benefit and only adds overhead' for CPU-bound work, while I/O-bound Workers de-schedule while waiting
notes: Key and all three distractors stand; option 2's 'extra threads never help beyond that' is false for I/O-bound pool work per the same guide.

fields.hint: Pass the flag to a one-line script and watch two things: what Node prints on stderr, and whether the script's own output still appears.
fields.explanation: --inspect activates the V8 inspector on 127.0.0.1:9229 and prints 'Debugger listening on ws://127.0.0.1:9229/…'; the process then speaks the Chrome DevTools Protocol, so Chrome DevTools, VS Code or another IDE can attach while the program runs normally. The variant that stops before the first line is --inspect-brk. The flag changes nothing about optimization, logging or NODE_ENV, and it binds to localhost precisely because an open inspector port is remote code execution.

fields.explanation: Node defines strictEqual as testing equality 'as determined by Object.is()', which is SameValue rather than ===. The difference is visible in exactly two places: assert.strictEqual(NaN, NaN) passes although NaN === NaN is false, and assert.strictEqual(0, -0) throws an AssertionError although 0 === -0 is true. Coercing == is what the legacy assert.equal uses, and recursive property comparison is deepStrictEqual — which also compares primitives with Object.is.

evidence: node: assert.strictEqual(NaN,NaN) PASSED (no throw); assert.strictEqual(0,-0) THREW AssertionError 'Expected values to be strictly equal'; raw NaN===NaN false and 0===-0 true; Object.is(NaN,NaN) true and Object.is(0,-0) false; assert.deepStrictEqual(NaN,NaN) passed while deepStrictEqual({a:0},{a:-0}) threw; assert.equal('1',1) passed (Node 22.22.2)

https://nodejs.org/docs/latest-v22.x/api/assert.html (v22.23.2): 'Tests strict equality between the actual and expected parameters as determined by Object.is()' with the documented failing example assert.strictEqual(0, -0); assert.equal is labelled 'Stability: 3 - Legacy' and uses the == operator; deepStrictEqual: 'Primitive values are compared using Object.is()'
notes: The Object.is rewrite is correct on both counts and the ===-claiming option is now a distractor; no other item in this batch repeats the === claim (186 mentions strictEqual only as an AssertionError source).

fields.hint: createReadStream hands over 64 KB at a time; readFile resolves with one Buffer holding everything. Ask what that changes and what it does not.
fields.explanation: createReadStream hands the file over in chunks that are collected once handled, so only a small window is resident: reading a 200 MB file lifted peak RSS about 40 MB above the process baseline through a stream, against about 200 MB with fs.promises.readFile, which materializes one 200 MB Buffer. Peak memory is what decides whether several concurrent large files fit in a container's limit. The same bytes still leave the disk, streaming makes more syscalls rather than fewer, and it does not shorten the total read — what it improves is when the first chunk can be processed.

problems: the absolute figures did not reproduce (282 MB measured 244 MB here); only the delta over the process baseline is machine-independent, so the claim is restated as a delta

node: stream.readableHighWaterMark is 65536, so 64 KB per chunk is exact
notes: Key and all three distractors verified; the deltas (+41-44MB streaming, +202MB readFile) reproduce on any baseline.

fields.explanation: require() returns whatever module.exports refers to when the file finishes executing. `exports` is only a local variable initialized to that same object, so exports.foo = 1 works, but `exports = { a: 1 }` repoints the local and leaves module.exports untouched: requiring such a file returned {}, while the module.exports version returned { a: 1 }. `export default` is ESM syntax and is a SyntaxError in a CommonJS file, and `global` is process-wide state, not a module's public surface.

evidence: node: a module containing `exports = { a: 1 }` required as {}; `module.exports = { a: 1 }` required as {"a":1}; `exports.a = 1` required as {"a":1} (Node 22.22.2)

node: `export default 1` in an unambiguous CommonJS file (.cjs, or .js under "type":"commonjs") threw SyntaxError: Unexpected token 'export'; note that in a bare .js with no package type Node 22 detects ESM and require() succeeds, so the explanation's 'in a CommonJS file' qualifier is doing real work and is correct
notes: Hint says 'one of the two' without naming which two, which is loose but inferable; left alone as the smaller change.

fields.explanation: Promise.all waits for every promise and resolves with an array in input order: three independent 150 ms jobs finished in 150 ms, while awaiting them one at a time took 452 ms. It rejects as soon as any input rejects, so reach for Promise.allSettled when you need every outcome including the failures. Promise.race and Promise.any settle on a single result — the first to settle, and the first to fulfill — so neither gives you all three values.

evidence: node: Promise.all of three 150ms jobs resolved ["a","b","c"] in 150ms and 151ms over two runs; the same three awaited in a for…of loop took 451ms and 452ms; Promise.all rejected after 0ms on a rejecting input while allSettled returned fulfilled,rejected in 151ms; Promise.race returned "a" and Promise.any returned "b", single values (Node 22.22.2)
notes: Both quoted timings reproduce exactly; the em-dash pair is a single parenthetical, not a chain, so it stays.
